chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Hamdan ibn Ibrahim al-Hamdani, raised it to one of the two Imams (peace be upon them).
He said: 'I love for the man that there be a debt upon him, intending its repayment.'

key_terms.الصَّادِقِينَ: The Truthful Ones (title for the 5th and 6th Imams)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual significance of having a debt according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Kafi, the Imam (peace be upon him) highlights the spiritual merit of carrying debt with the sincere intention of repayment, framing financial obligation not merely as a burden but as a means of cultivating discipline and accountability. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the moral dimension of transactions, where the intent (niyyah) transforms a worldly duty into an act of worship. The narration underscores that the struggle to fulfill one's dues is valued by God, encouraging believers to view debt as an opportunity for spiritual growth rather than solely as a financial liability.

en.hubeali:
Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Hamdan Bin Ibrahim Al Hamdany, 
(It has been narrated) raising it to one of the two truthful ones (5<sup>th</sup> or 6<sup>th</sup> Imam<sup>asws</sup>)
having said: ‘I<sup>asws</sup> love it for the man there happen to be debts upon him, intending its fulfilment (payment)’.
en.sarwar: 3. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Musa ibn Bakr who has said the following: “Abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, said to me, ‘Whoever works to provide sustenance for himself and his family is considered a Mujahid (fighter) for the cause of Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious.

If poverty over-powers him, he then should borrow upon the responsibility of Allah and His Messenger for his sustenance and his family. If he dies and cannot pay back, it then becomes the responsibility of the Imam to pay it. If he did not do so, he will be held responsible. Allah, most Majestic, most Glorious, says, ‘Charities are for the poor, destitute and the charity (tax) collectors . . . ., and those suffering bankruptcy.’ [9:61] He is poor, destitute and bankrupt.’”
